lines.text: Business communication in English operates across a spectrum of formality, from casual Slack messages to formal board reports, and mastering this range is essential for professional success. Email remains the backbone of written business communication: a clear subject line, appropriate greeting ('Dear Mr Khan' formal; 'Hi Sarah' informal), structured body paragraphs, and a professional sign-off ('Kind regards', 'Best wishes', 'Yours faithfully' for unknown recipients). Telephone communication has its own conventions: identifying yourself ('This is James calling from...'), stating the purpose ('I'm calling regarding...'), and closing ('Thank you for your time. I'll follow up by email.'). Presentations require confident delivery: opening hooks, signposting ('Firstly... Secondly... Finally...'), data interpretation ('As you can see from the graph...'), and strong closings with calls to action. Reports follow standardised structures: executive summary, methodology, findings, conclusions, and recommendations. Memos — brief internal communications — use a header format (To, From, Date, Subject) and get straight to the point. Business letters, while increasingly rare, still matter for contracts, formal complaints, and legal correspondence. Digital communication adds new channels: instant messaging (brief, conversational), video calls (camera etiquette, screen sharing), and collaborative documents (commenting, suggesting edits). The key skill is register-switching — knowing when to write 'Per our earlier conversation' versus 'As we discussed' versus 'Like I said'. Getting the tone wrong can damage relationships, undermine credibility, or create costly misunderstandings.

lines.text: British email culture values brevity and politeness. Opening with 'I hope this email finds you well' is standard (though increasingly parodied). 'Best wishes' is the safe all-purpose closing. Reply-all is used cautiously — unnecessary reply-alls are a common office complaint.
lines.name: British email culture values brevity and politeness. Opening with 'I hope this email finds you well' is standard (though increasingly parodied). 'Best wishes' is the safe all-purpose closing. Reply-all is used cautiously — unnecessary reply-alls are a common office complaint.

lines.text: Understanding CC (carbon copy — visible to all) and BCC (blind carbon copy — hidden) is culturally important. BCC-ing someone's boss is considered underhand; CC-ing creates accountability. 'Looping in' and 'copying in' are the conversational terms.
lines.name: Understanding CC (carbon copy — visible to all) and BCC (blind carbon copy — hidden) is culturally important. BCC-ing someone's boss is considered underhand; CC-ing creates accountability. 'Looping in' and 'copying in' are the conversational terms.

lines.text: British business culture generally prefers email for records but phones for urgency or relationship-building. 'Can I give you a quick ring about this?' signals the matter is either urgent or sensitive. Calling without prior email is less common than it used to be.

lines.text: This British convention is strictly observed in formal letters: 'Yours faithfully' when you don't know the recipient's name (Dear Sir/Madam). 'Yours sincerely' when you do (Dear Mr Smith). Getting it wrong in a job application or legal letter looks careless.
lines.name: This British convention is strictly observed in formal letters: 'Yours faithfully' when you don't know the recipient's name (Dear Sir/Madam). 'Yours sincerely' when you do (Dear Mr Smith). Getting it wrong in a job application or legal letter looks careless.

lines.text: British out-of-office messages follow a format: dates of absence, reason (brief), alternative contact, and return date. Humorous out-of-office messages ('I'm on a beach ignoring your email') are increasingly common but controversial in formal organisations.

lines.text: 'Dear Sir/Madam' is only for unknown recipients. If you know their name, use it. Using 'Dear Sir' when you know them seems cold and impersonal.
lines.name: 'Dear Sir/Madam' is only for unknown recipients. If you know their name, use it. Using 'Dear Sir' when you know them seems cold and impersonal.

lines.text: British convention: 'Yours faithfully' after 'Dear Sir/Madam' (unknown). 'Yours sincerely' after 'Dear Mr/Ms...' (known). Mix these up and it looks unprofessional.
lines.name: British convention: 'Yours faithfully' after 'Dear Sir/Madam' (unknown). 'Yours sincerely' after 'Dear Mr/Ms...' (known). Mix these up and it looks unprofessional.
